searchText: how many people can be on team 2 Hey folx, Sent my app in on the 14th, interested in seeing what I can learn! Thank you. I get the map of topics discussed in the community. Let's imagine that a large portion of people here are keen on learning about the application layer. Would you think it makes more sense to just keep the core dev apprenticeship program tightly bound to the original scope, or to also funnel it with a wider ecosystem apprenticeship call-to-arms? e.g. there are firms looking for solidity devs, and there are people on the verge of becoming solidity devs. The scope of the apprenticeship program isn't to work on applications. Are those applicants pointed elsewhere, and if so should we start organising a good elsewhere? dumb question: what's the reason the gas is charged for code execution? I get the reason to charge gas for accessing state, but why charge for instructions executed? CPU/memory cost of actually executing transactions has to be negligible compared to PoW, and we only do <20 TPS PoW only has to be generated by one person in the world per block, and it can be parallelized very easily. Block execution has to be done by *everyone* who runs an Ethereum client (which ideally would be everyone who uses Ethereum). fair point, but with so few TPS (and no plans to really increase TPS per node) CPU/memory/stack-only operations don't seem to be a big deal. full nodes already require substantial amount of CPU/memory, and it is most likely already dominated by internal node state management I guess another argument would be that we still want to cap the run time of each transaction, and charging gas per instruction executed makes sense. this brings another question: why different non-state-management instructions have different costs. (and another question is: is there **another** way of capping the run time? perhaps not) We have to consider user experience as well. In a perfect world, we would have separate costs for network utilization, CPU usage, and storage. However, users struggle enough already with a single fee type, adding 2 more will make it incredibly difficult for users to understand. Maybe if EIP-1559 goes over well we can make it so storage is fully charged with a basefee like mechanic, and leave network, CPU, and disk access bundled (since they are things that impact miner profitability). that's precisely my argument: why not roll all non-storage related opcodes into a single category and give all of them a fixed price (maybe even 0, but that will need another change)? as of now, I see all non-storage related opcodes having **different** gas gost And perhaps if some sort of stateless transactions are introduced we can further adjust. Some non zero amount of the applicants either misunderstood the intent of the program or potentially will be better served by learning the application layer first. We'll be looking for how to point those people in a useful/actionable direction. there are 2 point I'm trying to make 1: what happens if we set gas price for all non-state related opcodes to 1? Someone may answer but I would encourage you to go look for yourself You seem to have some strong opinions but are missing the base knowledge to really have an informed opinion. Going and doing the hard part of really understanding the evm and gas mechanics will be worth it The way to think about all such problems is to ask yourself, "how could I attack the network if X changed". Or in some cases, "how can I attack the network right now" (like in the pre-Berlin situation). Every change to Ethereum has to take that line of questioning very seriously. It is trivial to build a system that isn't resilient to attack. Building it so it is resilient to motivated and well funded attackers is the really hard part. This question is also testable. I'm from Argentina but moved to the Spanish Pyrenees a few months ago. <@!759053369616236595> welcome 🙂 continuing on this thread using this as a quick and dirty benchmark (it has flaws, but bear with me) ``` function warm_me_up( uint iterations ) external view returns (uint256) { uint256 ret; for (uint i = 0; i < iterations; i += 1) { ret += i; ret *= i; ret |= (i); ret = addmod(ret, i, 0xffffffffffffffffff); ret = mulmod(ret, i, 0xffffffffffffffffff); } return ret; } ``` with stock client, and I can do ~50k iterations in ~150ms (this is obviously hw dependant) with entire block's worth of gas (15M) with W{base,verylow,low,mid,high} reduced to 1, I can do ~160k iterations (this is not important) in ~550ms (this is important). **I can use up entire block's gas with cpu-only operations in only 0.5s. **. excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: PoW only has to be generated by one person in the world per block, and it can be parallelized very easily.  Block execution has to be done by *everyone* who runs an Ethereum client (which ideally would be everyone who uses Ethereum).

excerpts.author: owleksiyowpckcr
excerpts.content:
fair point, but with so few TPS (and no plans to really increase TPS per node) CPU/memory/stack-only operations don't seem to be a big deal. full nodes already require substantial amount of CPU/memory, and it is most likely already dominated by internal node state management

I guess another argument would be that we still want to cap the run time of each transaction, and charging gas per instruction executed makes sense. this brings another question: why different non-state-management instructions have different costs. (and another question is: is there **another** way of capping the run time? perhaps not)

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We have to consider user experience as well.  In a perfect world, we would have separate costs for network utilization, CPU usage, and storage.  However, users struggle enough already with a single fee type, adding 2 more will make it incredibly difficult for users to understand.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Maybe if EIP-1559 goes over well we can make it so storage is fully charged with a basefee like mechanic, and leave network, CPU, and disk access bundled (since they are things that impact miner profitability).

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content:
That's my interpretation as well. Two is going to be the default. I'm hesitant to do solo because being "alone" on a problem sucks. I'm hesitant to do more than two because I want to keep things simple and have easy 1:1 peer accountability.

But there are almost always situations where the "rules" don't make sense when it comes to squishy human stuff, so if you think you have a compelling reason to be a 1-person team or an >2-person team I am willing to have that conversation

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content: Yes, assuming things go well, the goal is to evolve this into a rolling thing where new cohorts start while previous cohorts are still active. Each cohort improves the documentation and onboarding material. Goal is to build a smooth on ramp for learning about and contributing to the protocol. Applicants from previous cohorts will be considered for future cohorts so everyone here who has applied  will be in the pool of candidates for the second cohort (cohort-one).

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content:
This is great, thanks for sharing! <@456226577798135808> under "Benefits", you are missing a few:
1. Have an up-to-date, canonical specification for the Ethereum protocol. The Yellowpaper lags behind the most recent hard forks, so the "spec" today is "YP + EIPs from hard forks not yet included in YP"
2. Post-merge (or when the merge is being spec'ed) having a harmonized Ethereum spec (eth2.0-specs + this new eth1 spec) would reduce confusion by a lot. 
3. Automatically generate tests from the new eth1 spec. Current tests for Eth1 are here: https://github.com/ethereum/tests/
